newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel Treasury's proposed reforms draw union fire.
newsitem.headline: Israel Treasury's proposed reforms draw union fire.

text.p: Israel's Treasury presented the government on Thursday with a plan to accelerate economic growth, drawing immediate threats of a nationwide strike by trade unions alarmed by the prospect of structural reforms.
The cabinet will discuss the proposals, which contained no surprises and covered privatisation, capital market reform and foreign currency liberalisation, on Sunday.
It was unclear when ministers would vote on the plan.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had asked the Treasury to draw up a plan aimed at reviving economic growth after rejecting its forecast that gross domestic product would increase by only 3-3.5 percent in 1998.
GDP is expected to expand only 2.5 percent this year after surging by more than six percent annually for most of the decade.

"If the government accepts on Sunday unilateral decisions on structural changes in the economy...we will convene and decide on a course of action up to a total strike with no time limits," Shlomo Shani, a senior Histadrut Trade Unions Federation official, told reporters.

The Treasury proposals, released to the media, set a minimum privatisation target for 1998 of four billion shekels ($1.1 billion), including the sale of the government's controlling shares in Israel's main commercial banks. Receipts will be used to fund debt.
Israel set a four billion shekel privatisation target for this year but hopes the sale of a controlling stake in Bank Hapoalim will raise the sum to seven billion shekels.

The government's sale last month of more shares in the main telecommunications company, Bezeq Israel Telecom, led to a one-day nationwide strike by 60,000 state workers and disruption of the telephone service.
The Histadrut complained at the time that Bezeq workers were not consulted about plans to privatise more of the company through a $250 million sale of 12.5 percent of its stock to Merrill Lynch.
Recommendations in the Treasury plan to increase competition in industries dominated by state-owned companies with powerful workers' committees were likely to sound alarm bells in the Histadrut.

Under the proposals, the Israel Electric Corporation's transmission monopoly for large customers would end, the cement market and bus services would be opened to competition and Israeli airlines other than state-owned carrier El Al could fly selected domestic and foreign routes.

The plan also called for a 20 percent increase in investment in infrastructure in 1998 to 13.1 billion shekels. The extra money would go mainly to public transport and roads, railroad expansion, sewage and water works and natural gas projects.
The Treasury programme revised a capital market reform plan shelved by the cabinet because of a controversial proposal to tax short-term savings. The new plan omits such a levy.

"The capital markets in Israel are beset by a number of structural problems. The institutional investors, pension funds and life insurance companies -- the backbone of healthy capital markets throughout the world -- are outside the markets in Israel," the document said.

The Treasury called for further liberalisation of the foreign currency market but gave no details other than to recommend the central bank proceed towards making the shekel fully convertible by mid-1998.
Under the proposals, a natural gas tender for a natural gas operator would be issued by February 1, 1998.
The plan envisages tightening controls on unemployment payments and fixing a 7,500 shekel fine on every foreign worker employed without a licence.
